title: Infrastructure pillars
prompt_markdown: Which set contains the three infrastructure pillars introduced in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: Git, Terraform, and Ansible

options.label: B
options.text: Compute, storage, and network

options.label: C
options.text: Development, testing, and production

options.label: D
options.text: Applications, users, and source code

grader_markdown: Compute executes workloads, storage retains data, and networking connects components. The other choices name tools, environments, or application-level concerns.

title: Declarative configuration
prompt_markdown: Which statement best describes a declarative infrastructure definition?

options.label: A
options.text: It records every command an administrator previously executed.

options.label: B
options.text: It specifies the exact order of all API calls that a tool must make.

options.label: C
options.text: It describes the desired state, while a tool works out how to reach it.

options.label: D
options.text: It guarantees that every operation can run in parallel.

grader_markdown: A declarative definition expresses the intended state. The tool determines the required operations from that definition and the current state. Declarative syntax does not mean every operation is independent or can run concurrently.

title: Idempotence
prompt_markdown: An automation run has successfully reached the desired state. Its inputs and the relevant external state then remain unchanged. What should a second idempotent run do?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the managed state unchanged because it already satisfies the declaration.

options.label: B
options.text: Recreate all resources to prove they can be recreated.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip checking the current state and report success.

options.label: D
options.text: Add another copy of each declared resource.

grader_markdown: Once the declaration is satisfied, repeating the operation under unchanged conditions should not further alter the managed state. Checking state is compatible with idempotence; duplicating or needlessly rebuilding resources is not required.

title: Cloud service models
prompt_markdown: A team moves from managing virtual machines under IaaS to a managed application platform under PaaS. Which responsibility would typically move towards the provider?

options.label: A
options.text: Deciding the application's business requirements

options.label: B
options.text: Maintaining the team's application source code

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing which application features to release

options.label: D
options.text: Maintaining more of the underlying operating system and runtime platform

grader_markdown: PaaS typically transfers more operating-system and runtime-platform maintenance to the provider. The exact responsibility boundary depends on the service. The team still owns its application requirements and code.

title: Why keep infrastructure definitions in Git
prompt_markdown: Give two benefits of version-controlling infrastructure definitions beyond simply having a backup copy. Explain how each benefit helps a team deliver changes reliably.
grader_markdown:
Award **1 mark each** for two benefits connected to reliable delivery, for example:

- A reviewable change history helps identify what changed, who changed it, and why.
- Pull requests and review help catch mistakes before applying changes.
- Automated validation can run against proposed configuration changes.
- A shared definition reduces undocumented manual differences between environments.
- A known earlier definition helps investigate or plan recovery from a bad change.

Do not award a separate benefit for “having another copy.” Reverting a Git commit does not by itself restore deleted data or guarantee a safe infrastructure rollback.

title: Configuration drift
prompt_markdown: Two servers were created from the same definition. An administrator later changes a setting manually on only one server. Explain what configuration drift means in this situation and describe one way to detect or reconcile it.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Actual managed configuration has diverged from its declared or intended state; the manually changed server now differs from that baseline.
- **1 mark:** Compare actual state with the definition, for example through a plan, configuration inspection, or a configuration-management run. Investigate whether the manual change is legitimate, then either update the reviewed declaration or reapply the intended configuration.

title: Mutable and immutable infrastructure
prompt_markdown: A server needs a new operating-system configuration. Contrast an in-place mutable update with an immutable replacement. Explain what must happen to persistent application data when using the replacement approach.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Mutable updates modify the existing server; immutable updates create a replacement from a newly prepared definition or image and switch the workload to it.
- **1 mark:** Preserve persistent data separately or use a tested backup/migration/restore procedure before retiring the old server. Replacement must not discard the only copy of application data.

title: Tool responsibilities in demo 01
prompt_markdown: In `demo-01`, `main.tf` creates an EC2 instance and writes an Ansible inventory; `playbook.yml` installs and configures Nginx. Explain the distinct responsibilities of Terraform and Ansible in this workflow.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** In this demo, Terraform defines and provisions AWS resources and produces connection information, including the inventory.
- **1 mark:** Ansible connects to the target and manages software, files, and service configuration inside the operating system.

These are the roles of the tools in this particular workflow, not an assertion that Ansible cannot manage cloud resources. `demo-03a` demonstrates that it can.

title: Dependencies and generated inventory
prompt_markdown:
Consider these excerpts from `demo-01/main.tf`:

```hcl
# Within aws_instance.server
key_name               = aws_key_pair.main_key.key_name
vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.main_security_group.id]
```

```yaml
# Within the Terraform-generated inventory template
ansible_host: ${aws_instance.server.public_ip}
```

1. Identify the two resources that the instance references and explain what those references tell Terraform about dependency ordering. **(2 marks)**
2. Explain why generating `ansible_host` from the instance output is more reliable than copying an IP address into a separate inventory by hand. Include what must happen to the inventory when a replacement instance receives a new public IP. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** `aws_key_pair.main_key` is referenced for the instance's SSH key-pair name.
- **1 mark:** `aws_security_group.main_security_group` is referenced for the attached security-group ID. Both resource references contribute implicit dependencies, so Terraform must obtain the required resource values before completing the dependent operation. Moving blocks up or down the file is not the dependency mechanism.
- **1 mark:** Using `aws_instance.server.public_ip` connects the inventory to the provisioned instance's actual output and avoids a separately maintained, potentially stale IP address.
- **1 mark:** Apply/regenerate the inventory after replacement and use that updated inventory for Ansible. A previously copied inventory does not update itself simply because a new instance exists.

Technical reference: [Terraform references and dependencies](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/references).

title: Predicting a repeated run
prompt_markdown:
The following is a shortened version of tasks in `demo-01/playbook.yml`:

```yaml
- name: Install nginx
  apt:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Create custom index.html
  copy:
    content: "Course homepage\n"
    dest: /var/www/html/index.html

- name: Start and enable nginx
  systemd:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: yes
```

Assume the first run succeeds and all relevant inputs remain unchanged.

1. Predict the effect of a second run on the package, file, and service. Explain why this illustrates idempotence. **(2 marks)**
2. Someone then manually changes the contents of `index.html`. What should the next run do, and why? **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** The installed package remains present; the matching file does not need rewriting; a running and enabled service remains in that state.
- **1 mark:** This is idempotence: once the requested state is reached, repetition with unchanged relevant inputs does not produce additional managed-state changes. The shown `state: present` does not mean “upgrade to whatever version is newest.”
- **1 mark:** A manual edit makes the managed file differ from the declared content, so the next successful `copy` task restores the declared contents.
- **1 mark:** The restoration reconciles drift against the declaration. It does not require replacing the whole server or reinstalling Nginx.

title: Image and running machine
prompt_markdown: What is the relationship between a machine image and a virtual machine?

options.label: A
options.text: The image is the live machine's current CPU and memory usage.

options.label: B
options.text: One image can be used to initialize multiple VM instances, which can later develop different state.

options.label: C
options.text: Every image can initialize only one VM.

options.label: D
options.text: Launching a VM automatically updates the source image whenever the VM changes.

grader_markdown: An image supplies the starting state for instances. The instances can subsequently change independently; their changes do not automatically rewrite the source image.

title: Packer output
prompt_markdown: What is the principal artifact produced by the AWS Packer build in `demo-02`?

options.label: A
options.text: A continuously reconciled Kubernetes deployment

options.label: B
options.text: A Terraform state file describing the production fleet

options.label: C
options.text: An Ansible inventory containing all running servers

options.label: D
options.text: A custom AMI built using a temporary instance

grader_markdown: The Packer build prepares a temporary instance and captures a reusable AMI. It does not, by itself, operate the long-lived production fleet.

title: Rebuildability
prompt_markdown: The lecture describes a problematic form of a “golden image.” What makes that example an anti-pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The image was modified manually and cannot be reliably recreated from a maintained build definition.

options.label: B
options.text: The organization uses a shared base image.

options.label: C
options.text: The image has been tested before use.

options.label: D
options.text: The image is generated by an automated build pipeline.

grader_markdown: The problem is the unrepeatable manual creation process and accumulated hidden changes. The lecturer explicitly distinguishes this from an automated, rebuildable image that an organization may also call a “golden image.” The name alone is not the anti-pattern.

title: Regions and architectures
prompt_markdown: A team needs equivalent Ubuntu-based machines in two AWS regions and on both x86-64 and ARM64 processors. Which assumption is sound?

options.label: A
options.text: One AMI ID is valid in every region and on both architectures.

options.label: B
options.text: The VM instance type converts any image to the required architecture automatically.

options.label: C
options.text: The team must select suitable images for each region and architecture combination.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the size of the VM's disk determines whether the image can boot.

grader_markdown: Image selection must match the target region and CPU architecture. Equivalent image contents in different regions do not imply the same AMI ID.

title: Stock and custom images
prompt_markdown: Explain the difference between a stock image and a custom image. Give one reason an organization would maintain a custom image instead of configuring every new machine entirely from a stock image at launch time.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A stock image is a supplied starting image, such as a distribution vendor's Ubuntu image; a custom image adds an organization's chosen software or configuration.
- **1 mark:** A relevant reason, such as consistently applying a security baseline, reducing repeated installation work, shortening launch time, or maintaining a tested organization-specific starting state.

title: Build time and boot time
prompt_markdown: Explain the difference between Packer provisioning during an image build and cloud-init configuration when a machine boots. Give one suitable example for each stage.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Packer provisioning prepares the image before it is reused, for example installing shared tooling or applying a common baseline.
- **1 mark:** Cloud-init can initialize an instance at boot using supplied metadata/user data, for example setting instance-specific configuration or running initial setup. It is not a general continuously running reconciliation loop; whether an individual action repeats depends on cloud-init configuration and module frequency.

Accept reasonable alternative placements if the student explains the trade-off between a larger prepared baseline and more work at launch.

title: Containers and virtual machines
prompt_markdown: Explain one important difference between a typical Linux container and a virtual machine in how they use the operating-system kernel. State one practical consequence for their isolation or compatibility.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Typical Linux containers share the host's Linux kernel, while VMs run a guest operating system with its own kernel over virtualized hardware.
- **1 mark:** A valid consequence: containers generally have a smaller startup/runtime overhead, share a kernel-level boundary, or require compatibility with the host kernel. VMs can provide different guest kernels. On a non-Linux desktop, Linux containers normally use a Linux VM underneath.

Do not accept “containers have no isolation” or “any container can run unchanged on any operating system and architecture.”

title: Image layers
prompt_markdown: A company needs web-server and database-server images with the same security baseline. Propose a simple image hierarchy and explain one maintenance benefit compared with independently repeating the baseline setup in every image build.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A suitable hierarchy is vendor Ubuntu → shared organization baseline → separate web and database images.
- **1 mark:** Shared baseline changes can be maintained centrally and reused, reducing duplicated provisioning logic and inconsistent baseline setup. Descendant images still need rebuilding and testing when the baseline changes; existing instances do not inherit the changes automatically.

title: Reading the image build
prompt_markdown:
`demo-02/devops-ubuntu-26.04-aws.pkr.hcl` defines two build sources:

```hcl
source "amazon-ebs" "ubuntu-north" {
  region = "eu-north-1"
  # Other settings omitted
}

source "amazon-ebs" "ubuntu-west" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
  # Other settings omitted
}

# The build uses both sources. Its provisioning scripts include,
# in this order:
# cloud-init.sh, base.sh, git.sh, aws-cli.sh, motd.sh,
# disable-auto-updates.sh, cleanup.sh, zerodisk.sh
```

The first script waits for the initial cloud-init process to finish. The final scripts clean temporary files and prepare the disk before the image is captured.

1. Describe the build lifecycle from source image to resulting AMI, including the role of the temporary VM and what happens to it after a successful build. **(2 marks)**
2. Why does the build wait for cloud-init before changing the operating system, and why does cleanup belong after software installation? **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** For each configured source, Packer starts a temporary VM from the selected stock image and runs the provisioners against it.
- **1 mark:** It captures the prepared machine state as a custom AMI and, on normal successful completion, removes the temporary build instance. The two configured targets produce regional AMIs; the image artifacts remain available.
- **1 mark:** Waiting for cloud-init avoids racing initial configuration, package-manager activity, or related boot-time setup.
- **1 mark:** Final cleanup removes build-time leftovers after installation has finished, so temporary files and caches are not needlessly captured in the reusable image. Cleanup is not proof that every secret or machine-specific identity has been sanitized.

title: Repeating a build and rolling out an update
prompt_markdown:
The Packer template selects its source image using `most_recent = true`. Its `base.sh` script runs `apt-get update` and `apt-get dist-upgrade`. A student claims: “The code is in Git, so rebuilding next month is guaranteed to produce exactly the same software versions.”

1. Assess that claim. Identify two inputs that can change without a change to the Git commit, and explain how to control them when reproducible versions are required. **(2 marks)**
2. The team deliberately builds a patched image. Describe an immutable rollout to the running application, including validation and preservation of persistent data. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** `most_recent = true` can resolve to a different source AMI later. Record or pin the approved source AMI for the relevant region/architecture when rebuilding the same version is required.
- **1 mark:** Package repositories and the versions selected by `dist-upgrade` can change. Control approved package versions and their availability, for example with a versioned repository snapshot or equivalent reproducible dependency source. Versioned build instructions alone do not freeze external inputs.
- **1 mark:** Build and validate the patched image, then create replacement instances and verify application health before directing traffic to them. Retain an appropriate recovery path until the replacement is proven.
- **1 mark:** Keep persistent application data on suitable separately managed storage or migrate/restore it through a tested procedure before retiring old instances. Running machines are not patched merely by publishing a new AMI.

title: Inventory
prompt_markdown: What is the main purpose of an Ansible inventory?

options.label: A
options.text: To store a binary snapshot of every server

options.label: B
options.text: To replace all role defaults and templates

options.label: C
options.text: To identify managed hosts and groups, with variables such as connection details

options.label: D
options.text: To record only the commands that previously failed

grader_markdown: Inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate variables such as SSH connection details with them.

title: Partial state
prompt_markdown: A playbook ensures that Nginx is installed but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you generally expect?

options.label: A
options.text: The unrelated package remains unless a task explicitly manages or removes it.

options.label: B
options.text: Ansible removes every package absent from the playbook.

options.label: C
options.text: Ansible recreates the server from a stock image.

options.label: D
options.text: The playbook must fail because the server has additional state.

grader_markdown: Ansible ordinarily manages the state expressed by the tasks. An omitted resource is not automatically declared absent; additional unmanaged state can remain.

title: Roles
prompt_markdown: Why does `demo-03a` separate `common`, `web`, `database`, and `batch` into roles?

options.label: A
options.text: Roles guarantee that all tasks run simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Each role creates its own independent Ansible installation.

options.label: C
options.text: Roles prevent the use of variables shared across hosts.

options.label: D
options.text: Roles package related tasks and supporting files so they can be organized and reused.

grader_markdown: Roles organize related tasks, defaults, templates, handlers, and other supporting resources into reusable units. They do not guarantee task parallelism or prohibit shared variables.

title: Variable precedence
prompt_markdown: Consider a simplified version of the demo's port configuration using a scalar variable named `app_port`. Role defaults set it to `8080`, the target host's group variables set it to `3000`, and the playbook command includes `-e app_port=9000`. What value should `{{ app_port }}` produce?

options.label: A
options.text: `8080`, because the role owns its configuration

options.label: B
options.text: `9000`, because the extra variable overrides the other supplied values

options.label: C
options.text: `3000`, because group variables always override command-line values

options.label: D
options.text: An error, because the same variable cannot appear in multiple places

grader_markdown:
The command-line extra variable sets `app_port` to `9000`. Extra variables have higher variable precedence than the group variables and role defaults in this example. Multiple definitions are permitted; precedence determines the effective value. The scalar form in the question avoids unrelated dictionary-merging details.

Technical reference: [Ansible variable precedence](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/playbook_guide/playbooks_variables.html#understanding-variable-precedence).

title: Selecting hosts and roles
prompt_markdown: In `demo-03a/provisioning/provision.yml`, the `common` role targets `fleet`, while the `web`, `database`, and `batch` roles target their respective host groups. Explain which roles a host belonging to `web_servers` should receive and why the grouping is useful.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A web host belongs to `web_servers`, which is a child group of `fleet`, so it receives the `common` role in the first play and the `web` role in the web play during a normal full run.
- **1 mark:** This applies a shared baseline to the fleet while limiting specialized configuration to the appropriate hosts. It avoids installing the entire database or batch stack everywhere.

title: Service state
prompt_markdown: Explain the difference between `state: started` and `enabled: yes` in a service task. Why is `state: restarted` different from `state: started` when a playbook is run repeatedly?
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** `state: started` requests that the service be running now, while `enabled: yes` requests that it start automatically at boot. These are distinct aspects of service state.
- **1 mark:** `state: restarted` requests a restart whenever the task executes, whereas `state: started` normally leaves an already running service running. Repeated restart operations can cause unnecessary disruption even if the final service state is “running.”

title: Registering results
prompt_markdown:
The infrastructure playbook in `demo-03a` uses:

```yaml
- name: Create web security group
  amazon.aws.ec2_security_group:
    # Other settings omitted
    state: present
  register: web_sg

# A later EC2 task uses:
# security_group: "{{ web_sg.group_id }}"
```

Explain what `register` does here and why the later task uses the returned group ID instead of a manually copied value. These are excerpts; no execution is required.
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** `register: web_sg` stores the task's returned result in a variable named `web_sg`, including its `group_id`.
- **1 mark:** Referencing that returned ID passes the actual created or located resource into the later task and avoids manually duplicating a changing cloud identifier. The producing task must execute before its result is consumed in this sequence.

title: Provisioning and testing
prompt_markdown: The demo separates `00_create.sh`, `50_provision.sh`, and `60_test.sh`. Explain the difference between creating infrastructure and provisioning its operating-system/application state. Why is a separate functional test useful even when provisioning exits successfully?
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** Creation establishes infrastructure such as instances, security groups, and connection information; provisioning installs/configures the operating-system and application resources on those instances.
- **1 mark:** Successful tasks do not prove that the application works end to end. Functional tests can check health endpoints, database access, or communication between components that might still be misconfigured.

title: Templates and handlers
prompt_markdown:
Consider this shortened excerpt from the web role in `demo-03a`:

```yaml
# tasks/main.yml
- name: Configure Nginx for web application
  template:
    src: nginx-site.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/{{ project_name }}
  notify:
    - reload nginx

# handlers/main.yml
- name: reload nginx
  systemd:
    name: nginx
    state: reloaded
```

Assume a successful play, no forced handler flushes, and no other task notifying this handler.

1. When should the handler run if rendering the template changes the destination file? What happens on the next run if the rendered file is identical? **(2 marks)**
2. Suppose three changed tasks notify the same handler before the normal end-of-tasks handler phase. How many times should it run in that phase, and why is this useful? **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** A changed template task notifies `reload nginx`; in the stated scenario it runs at the normal handler phase after the play's regular tasks.
- **1 mark:** If the rendered file is unchanged on the next run, that task does not notify the handler, so it does not cause a reload.
- **1 mark:** The same handler runs once in that handler phase despite three notifications.
- **1 mark:** Combining notifications avoids redundant reloads and lets the service consume the completed configuration changes together.

Technical reference: [Ansible handlers and notification timing](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/playbook_guide/playbooks_handlers.html). A later explicit flush or later handler phase changes the scope of the “once” statement; the question intentionally excludes that complication.

title: A misleading idempotence guard
prompt_markdown:
The web role contains this dependency-installation task:

```yaml
- name: Install Node.js dependencies
  shell: |
    cd "{{ app_directory }}"
    npm install
  become_user: "{{ app_user }}"
  args:
    creates: "{{ app_directory }}/node_modules"
```

The `node_modules` directory already exists from an earlier deployment. A new application release changes the required dependencies in `package.json`.

1. Predict whether this task runs and explain the resulting risk. **(2 marks)**
2. Propose a change-aware way to install updated dependencies and one check that would show the application has the intended dependency state. Simply forcing every task to report `ok` is not a solution. **(2 marks)**
grader_markdown:
- **1 mark:** The existing `node_modules` path causes `creates` to skip the shell command.
- **1 mark:** Directory existence does not prove that installed dependencies match the new manifest; the application can retain stale or missing dependencies.
- **1 mark:** Propose a manifest/lockfile-aware installation step, for example register changes to deployed dependency definitions and run a suitable installation task when those change or dependencies are missing. A committed lockfile with `npm ci` is one valid approach, if the required files and installation conditions are handled correctly. A checksummed build artifact is another defensible approach.
- **1 mark:** Verify installed dependency versions against the intended manifest/lockfile or run a targeted application/smoke test that exercises the changed dependency. A combination is strongest. Merely testing whether the directory exists does not establish dependency correctness.

Technical references: [Ansible shell creates guard](https://docs.ansible.com/projects/ansible/latest/collections/ansible/builtin/shell_module.html) and [npm ci requirements](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/commands/npm-ci/).
